assumptions: a. The airframe is assumed to be a rigid body.
b. The earth is assumed to be fixed in inertial space.
c. The mass and mass distribution of the vehicle are assumed to be constant.
d. The aircraft has a plane of symmetry.
e. Effects associated with rotation of the vertical relative to inertial space are assumed negligible; the magnitude of the gravity vector is assumed constant.

axis_systems.origin: All the axis systems have their origin at the aircraft center of gravity.
axis_systems.earth: Z along the local gravity vector; X_E, Y_E horizontal with arbitrary but fixed direction.
axis_systems.body: X_B positive forward along the fuselage reference line; Z_B in the plane of symmetry, positive down; Y_B positive out the right wing. Euler angles psi, theta, phi in that order. 'All angles and angular rates are positive in a righthanded sense.'
axis_systems.flight_path_or_wind: X_W along the total velocity VT; Z_W in the plane of symmetry; located from the body axes by alpha (rotation about Y_B) and beta (rotation about Z_W). Still air: flight-path axes = wind axes.
wind_to_body_equation_1: X_B = cos(alpha)cos(beta) X_W - cos(alpha)sin(beta) Y_W - sin(alpha) Z_W
Z_B = sin(alpha)cos(beta) X_W - sin(alpha)sin(beta) Y_W + cos(alpha) Z_W
axis_systems.alpha_beta_definitions_used_in_the_pilot: alpha = asin(w/VT), beta = asin(v/VT) (p.5), with the body-axis w-dot equation substituted for the alpha-dot equation because of the large excursions

equations: P_dot = (c1 R + c2 P) Q + c3 L + c4 N
Q_dot = c5 R P + c6 (R^2 - P^2) + c7 M
R_dot = (c8 P + c9 R) Q + c4 L + c10 N
alpha_dot = Q - tan(beta)(P cos(alpha) + R sin(alpha)) + Z_W/(m VT cos(beta))
beta_dot = P sin(alpha) - R cos(alpha) + Y_W/(m VT)
M = q S c Cm + z_j T
body_axis_moments_5.quote: Cl, Cm, and Cn are the total body-axis nondimensional aerodynamic moment coefficients (referenced to the c.m.). (p.6)

equations: X_W = T cos(beta) cos(alpha + xi_0) + m g {cos(theta) cos(phi) sin(alpha) cos(beta) - sin(theta) cos(alpha) cos(beta) + cos(theta) sin(phi) sin(beta)} + YA sin(beta) - D cos(beta)
Y_W = -T sin(beta) cos(alpha + xi_0) + m g {cos(theta) sin(phi) cos(beta) + sin(theta) cos(alpha) sin(beta) - cos(theta) cos(phi) sin(alpha) sin(beta)} + YA cos(beta) + D sin(beta)
Z_W = -T sin(alpha + xi_0) + m g {sin(theta) sin(alpha) + cos(theta) cos(phi) cos(alpha)} - L

aerodynamic_forces_7.quote: Lift, L, and drag, D, are assumed in the plane of symmetry; lift positive up and perpendicular to the velocity vector, drag positive aft and along the projection of the total velocity in the plane of symmetry. The side force YA is that component of the total aerodynamic force which is perpendicular to the plane of symmetry; it lies along the Y_B axis and is positive out the right wing.

table_1.title: TABLE 1. AERODYNAMIC COEFFICIENT EQUATIONS  a) Stability Axis Force Coefficients (PDF p.30, printed 14);  b) Body Axis Moment Coefficients (Concluded) (PDF p.31, printed 15)
table_1.form: hand-lettered; read once on the page image at two magnifications (the equations repeat the same pattern in each alpha range, which checks the reading)
table_1.notation: alpha, beta in degrees; delta_stab, delta_a, delta_sp, delta_r in degrees; p, q, r, alpha_dot in rad/sec; VT total velocity in ft/sec; b span and c mean aerodynamic chord in ft. F(x) means table function F looked up at x degrees; F(45) or F(110) means the end value is held.

rolling_moment.equation: Cl = Cl_beta_i(|alpha|)*beta + (b/(2*VT))*{Cl_p_j(|alpha|)*p + Cl_r(|alpha|)*r} + Cl_delta_a(|alpha|)*delta_a + Cl_delta_sp(|alpha|)*delta_sp + Cl_delta_r(|alpha|)*delta_r
Cl = Cl_beta_i(|alpha|)*beta + (b/(2*VT))*{Cl_p_j(45)*p + Cl_r(45)*r} + Cl_delta_a(45)*delta_a + Cl_delta_sp(45)*delta_sp + Cl_delta_r(45)*delta_r
Cl = Cl_beta_i(110)*beta + (b/(2*VT))*{Cl_p_j(45)*p + Cl_r(45)*r} + Cl_delta_a(45)*delta_a + Cl_delta_sp(45)*delta_sp + Cl_delta_r(45)*delta_r

pitching_moment.equation: Cm_REF = {Cm_BASIC(|alpha|)}*SGA + Delta_Cm_k(|alpha|, beta*) + (c/(2*VT))*{Cm_q(|alpha|)*q + Cm_alpha_dot(|alpha|)*alpha_dot} + {Cm_delta_stab(|alpha|) + K_beta*|beta|}*delta_stab + Cm_delta_a(|alpha|)*|delta_a| + Cm_delta_sp(|alpha|)*|delta_sp|

Cm_REF = {Cm_BASIC(|alpha|)}*SGA + Delta_Cm_k(45, beta*) + (c/(2*VT))*{Cm_q(45)*q + Cm_alpha_dot(45)*alpha_dot} + {Cm_delta_stab(|alpha|) + K_beta*|beta|}*delta_stab + Cm_delta_a(45)*|delta_a| + Cm_delta_sp(45)*|delta_sp|

Cm_REF = {Cm_BASIC(110)}*SGA + Delta_Cm_k(45, beta*) + (c/(2*VT))*{Cm_q(45)*q + Cm_alpha_dot(45)*alpha_dot} + {Cm_delta_stab(110) + K_beta*|beta|}*delta_stab + Cm_delta_a(45)*|delta_a| + Cm_delta_sp(45)*|delta_sp|

pitching_moment.note_as_printed: NOTE: for |beta| <= 30 deg, beta* = |beta|;  |beta| > 30 deg, beta* = 30 deg.  for alpha >= 0, SGA = 1;  for alpha < 0, SGA = -1
pitching_moment.K_beta: printed as K with subscript beta and superscript Cm_delta_stab; value in Table 3 (0.00011 per deg^2)

yawing_moment.equation: Cn_REF = Cn_beta_l(|alpha|)*beta + (b/(2*VT))*{Cn_p(|alpha|)*p + Cn_r(|alpha|)*r} + Cn_delta_a(|alpha|)*delta_a + Cn_delta_sp(|alpha|)*delta_sp + Cn_delta_r(|alpha|)*delta_r
Cn_REF = Cn_beta_l(45)*beta + (b/(2*VT))*{Cn_p(45)*p + Cn_r(45)*r} + Cn_delta_a(45)*delta_a + Cn_delta_sp(45)*delta_sp + Cn_delta_r(45)*delta_r

axes_and_reference.forces: CL, CD, Cy are 'stability-axis' force coefficients as the report uses the term (p.6-7): lift up and perpendicular to the velocity vector, in the plane of symmetry; drag aft along the projection of the velocity on the plane of symmetry; side force Cy along the body Y axis, positive out the right wing. For non-zero sideslip D and YA are therefore not the wind-axis X and Y forces (Fig. 2).
axes_and_reference.moments: Cl, Cm, Cn are body-axis moment coefficients: Cl and Cn made dimensional with q*S*b, Cm with q*S*c.
axes_and_reference.moment_reference: The tables give moments about the reference centre Xref = 31% c. The transfer to the actual c.g. is the last line of the pitch and yaw blocks: Cm = Cm_REF + ((Xcg - Xref)/100)*(CL*cos(alpha) + CD*sin(alpha)); Cn = Cn_REF + ((Xcg - Xref)/100)*(c/b)*Cy. With Xcg = 29.3 the factor (Xcg - Xref)/100 is -0.017. No transfer is applied to the rolling moment and no vertical c.g. offset is modelled.
axes_and_reference.nondimensional_rates: p and r with b/(2*VT); q and alpha_dot with c/(2*VT); rates in rad/sec (derivatives per radian).

summary: Base data: Ref. 16 (Teper and Johnston, 'F4J Data Package', Systems Technology, Inc., WP-2141-1, June 1977), covering alpha -5 to 31 deg and beta -10 to 10 deg.

Extension of the static coefficients to 110 deg: wind-tunnel tests of an F-4 model, Ref. 2 = NASA TN D-6425 (Anglin, 1971; alpha -10 to 110 deg, beta -40 to 40 deg), 'the primary sources for the extension of static coefficients'.

Dynamic (rate) coefficients: 'extrapolated based on trends of data available from other sources to 60 deg angle-of-attack, with the intent of making such coefficients simple to mechanize'. (The rate tables as listed stop at 45 deg and Table 1 holds the 45-deg value above that.)

Ref. 16 itself drew on three sources: (1) Ref. 3, Bowser's digitised 'F-4 High-AOA Data Package' from McDonnell MDC A0005 Vol. II, based on the spin-evaluation data of Ref. 4 (functions of alpha 0-90, beta 0-40, delta_stab -21 to 0 deg); (2) a NASA Langley tabulation based on several tunnel investigations, 'e.g., Refs. 5 and 6' = NASA TN D-5361 and TN D-6091 (alpha -10 to 120, beta -40 to +40 deg); both 'limited to the very low speed regime (M = 0.2)'; (3) Ref. 7, the NASA Langley Differential Maneuvering Simulator data for the F-4J and slatted F-4E (NASA TM X-2827), functions of alpha, M and H over -5 < alpha < 30 deg, .2 < M < 2.4, 15,000 < H < 45,000 ft, from which 'several key damping derivatives were updated'.

'As originally received, the data did not coalesce at 0.2 M. The data of Ref. 4 were therefore given the most weight at this low Mach and were smoothed into the DMS data by about 0.4 M.' Ref. 16 was judged 'an excellent model of the aircraft' over -4 < alpha < 30 deg, -10 < beta < 10 deg, 0.2 < M < 1.0, 0 < H < 25,000 ft.

Simplifications made for this appendix: 'normalizing the data for trim Mach Number (determined from previous digital simulations using the Ref. 16 data set), using a single altitude (15,000 ft), and defining values for the second set of the parameters Cl_beta, Cn_beta, Cl_p, and Delta Cm.'
data_sources.per_function_attribution: The report does not say which source each individual table came from. What it says is by group: static coefficients (CLBAS, CDBAS, CMBAS, CYB, CRB, CNB, Delta Cm, and the control effectiveness tables) from Ref. 16 to about 30 deg and from TN D-6425 trends beyond; rate derivatives (CRP, CRR, CNP, CNR, CMQ, CMAD) from Ref. 16 with DMS (TM X-2827) updates, extrapolated on trends; second sets (CRB2, CRP2, DCM2, CNB2) defined by the authors.
data_sources.mach_range: None in the tables: one value per alpha, 'normalized for trim Mach number' at 15,000 ft. The low-speed sources are M = 0.2; no compressibility terms.
data_sources.rigid_or_flexible: Not stated for the aerodynamic data. The equations of motion assume a rigid airframe (assumption a, p.1). The wind-tunnel sources are rigid models; whether Ref. 16's flight-range data carried flexibility corrections is not said.
data_sources.configuration: 'a relatively "clean" aircraft (no flap, slat, or gear deflection) based upon an F-4J, with external stores consisting of one centerline fuel tank and one air-to-air missile' (p.1). The F-4J is a hard-wing (unslatted) F-4. Stores appear only as Delta_CD_STORES = 0.0037. The validation table lists the F-4J model with an empty centerline tank and wing pylons 2 and 8.

quotes: No F-4J flight test traces of high AOA are available to compare against dynamics from the foregoing mathematical model.

The only high-AOA flight traces available are from the F-4E stall/post-stall flight test (Ref. 8). McDonnell Aircraft Co. indicates that all hard-wing models (no leading-edge slats) of the F-4 have approximately the same stall/departure characteristics.

The Air Force (Ref. 8) noted the longer nose F-4E to have somewhat less wing rock tendency than the C and D models. The F-4J is more similar to the C and D and therefore might also have more pronounced wing rock.

f4e_test_aircraft_vs_f4j_model.note: The F-4E test aircraft had a spin chute, a beefed-up aft fuselage and offsetting nose ballast.

wing_rock.quote: Reference 8 indicates that the clean aircraft exhibited lateral/directional stability breakdown in the form of a slightly divergent dutch roll (wing rock) in the vicinity of 19-22 deg AOA.
wing_rock.model: This also indicates that at zero sideslip the dutch roll slowly becomes divergent at about 19 deg AOA. (Fig. 29, the model's linearised roots)

nose_slice.quote: As AOA was further increased the motion progressed from primarily roll to yaw (nose slice) in the region of 22-25.5 deg AOA.
nose_slice.explanation_quote: The aero data plot, Fig. 23, shows that Cn_beta passes through zero at about 20 deg AOA, while at this same point Cl_beta (Fig. 10) is still relatively large. One would expect, then, that the dutch roll motion would be primarily rolling motion (wing rock). By 25 deg AOA Cl_beta is very small, while Cn_beta is very large negative. Thus, one would expect the dutch roll mode to be primarily one of yaw motion (nose slice).
nose_slice.check_against_table_9: CNB1 crosses zero at 18.4 deg (linear between +.0013 at 15 and -.0006 at 20); CRB1 is -.00118 at 20 and -.00006 at 25; CNB1 is -.0033 at 25 and -.0040 at 30.

figure_29.title: Figure 29. F-4J 6 DOF Linearized Equation; Lateral/Longitudinal Root Migration with alpha and beta
figure_29.content: root loci of the short period and dutch roll for alpha_0 = 20 to 26 deg and beta_0 = 0, 1.5 and 5.5 deg; at beta_0 = 0 the dutch roll pair meets the real axis at alpha = 26 deg (two real unstable roots marked 26). Not digitised.

flight.figure: Figure 30. Controls Fixed Wing Rock Time History (Ref. 8)
flight.quote: Figure 30 is an F-4E time trace from Ref. 8 at 21 deg AOA and with all augmentation off. (It also has trailing-edge flaps at half deflection but they have a relatively small influence on lateral/directional stability.) The traces show the dutch roll to be a constant-amplitude, limit-cycle-like oscillation.

simulation.figure: Figure 31. F-4J Open-Loop Nonlinear Airframe Response to Pulse Aileron; alpha_0 = 21 deg, beta_0 = 0 deg

quote_after.text: The absolute magnitude of motions depends upon the initial excitation and is not particularly close. However, the ratios of the motions are quite close and again tend to validate the aero model. The period of the oscillation is quite different because of the higher energy (dynamic pressure) of the flight test maneuver.

frequency_doubling.quote: This 'frequency doubling' can only be caused by the pitching moment due to sideslip, Cm_beta, which is quite strong and negative for the F-4 aircraft.
figures: Figure 32. Pull-Up and Steady Wing Rock (From Ref. 8), PDF p.64 (printed 48): F-4E traces of beta, phi, delta_r, delta_stk, theta, alpha; alpha climbs from about 17 to about 25 deg while the wing rock grows; yaw SAS on.
Figure 33. F-4J Wing Rock with Pitch and Yaw SAS On and alpha_0 = 23 deg, PDF p.65 (printed 49)
frequency_doubling.model_link: This is the Delta_Cm_k(alpha, |beta|) table (DCM1): nose-down with sideslip of either sign, hence twice per dutch-roll cycle.

departure_in_wind_up_turn.figure: Figure 34. Departure During Left Wind-Up Turn
departure_in_wind_up_turn.quote: A final comparison between flight and simulation is shown in Fig. 34. Both aircraft depart from a wind-up turn to the left.
departure_in_wind_up_turn.what_the_figure_shows: Two rows of small aircraft silhouettes at 0.5-second intervals ('Time -> 0.5 sec Intervals'), one labelled 'F-4E FLIGHT TEST' and one 'F-4J SIMULATION', each about 16 silhouettes (roughly 8 seconds), the attitude rolling and yawing away at the right-hand end.
departure_in_wind_up_turn.not_given: Figure 34 and its text give NO speed, Mach number, altitude, load factor, angle of attack, control inputs or time of departure. The only numbers are the 0.5-second spacing. The appendix's one stated flight condition is the reference altitude of 15,000 ft (Table 5); the wing-rock comparison notes the flight-test manoeuvre was a wind-up turn at 'higher energy (dynamic pressure)' than the straight-and-level simulation.

conclusion.quote: On the basis of the above it was considered that the aero model exhibits characteristics adequately representative of the F-4 aircraft for use in analysis and simulation of stall/departure.
